one_liner: Small asynchronous C++11 stream-style logger; lower median caller latency than spdlog async, far behind Quill/fmtlog/PlatformLab NanoLog.
what_it_does: NanoLog is a two-file (NanoLog.hpp plus NanoLog.cpp) asynchronous file logger with LOG_INFO / LOG_WARN / LOG_CRIT stream macros, run-time log level, and size-based file rolling. You call nanolog::initialize once with either a GuaranteedLogger (never drops lines) or a NonGuaranteedLogger(ring_mb) (fixed ring that overwrites old lines), and a background thread formats and writes to <dir><name>.N.txt. It is not a drop-in for spdlog: there are no sinks, no fmt-style format strings, no console output and only three levels.
how_it_is_fast: The calling thread only encodes raw binary arguments (timestamp, thread id, file/function pointers, then typed values) into a 256-byte NanoLogLine with an inline stack buffer, so string literals are stored as pointers (zero copy) and integer/double-to-text conversion is deferred to the consumer thread. The guaranteed mode pushes into a chain of 8 MB buffers of 32768 slots claimed with one relaxed fetch_add and a per-slot release flag; the non-guaranteed mode is a fixed MPSC ring of 256-byte cache-aligned slots, each guarded by a per-slot atomic_flag spinlock. Formatting with std::ostream, timestamp printing and file I/O all happen on the single background thread.
when_to_use: Legacy or C++11-only codebases that want an async file logger in two source files with no dependencies
Moderate-rate logging of short lines (under about 256 bytes, so no heap allocation per line) where median caller latency matters more than tail latency
As a readable reference design for deferred-formatting loggers (binary encode on the hot path, stringify on a worker)
When you can tolerate dropped lines and want a producer that never blocks on a full queue (NonGuaranteedLogger)
when_not_to_use: Latency-critical work today: in the Quill harness it trails Quill, fmtlog, XTR, MS BinLog and PlatformLab NanoLog by roughly 10x at the median, and its 4-thread 99.9th percentile (1419 ns) is worse than spdlog's (1106 ns)
When you need console sinks, custom formatting, local-time timestamps, appending to an existing file, or structured output: none are provided

Bursty high-volume logging in guaranteed mode: the producer that fills a buffer allocates the next 8 MB buffer in its own call, other producers spin, and memory grows without bound if the writer falls behind

Production systems that need a maintained project: abandoned since 2017-03-08 with 18 open issues, including #39 (2025) reporting producer blocking in NonGuaranteedLogger and lost final lines at shutdown in GuaranteedLogger

integration.platforms: any platform with a C++11 standard library; README numbers from Linux Mint 17 on x86-64
integration.thread_safety: Logging macros are safe to call from many threads after initialize(); one background thread consumes. Calling a LOG_ macro before initialize() dereferences a null logger pointer.

gotchas: License: GitHub shows none and no LICENSE file exists (issue #32), but both NanoLog.hpp and NanoLog.cpp open with the full MIT License text, Copyright (c) 2016 Karthik Iyengar, so the code is copyable under MIT with that notice kept.
Every log line is terminated with std::endl, which flushes the ofstream per line on the writer thread (issue #31); this caps writer throughput and was not part of the caller-latency benchmark.

The writer thread sleeps 50 us whenever the queue is empty, timestamps come from std::chrono::high_resolution_clock at microsecond resolution and are printed in UTC via std::gmtime (issues #11, #24, #39).

The README benchmark timed each call with a microsecond clock, so the 50th percentile of 0 us and the 0.35 us average are quantized; the Quill harness, which reports nanoseconds, is the more reliable comparison.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only when you want the smallest possible C++11 async logger to vendor or study; for real speed choose PlatformLab NanoLog, Quill or fmtlog, which beat it by about 10x at the median in the same Quill harness and are maintained.
verified_claims_summary: In the independent Quill benchmark (odygrd/logger_benchmarks, GCC 14.2, -march=x86-64-v3, i5-12600, logging two ints and a double) Iyengar NanoLog's caller latency is 106/155/491 ns at the 50th/90th/99.9th percentile with 1 thread versus spdlog 271/296/360 ns, and 73/267/1419 ns versus 557/614/1106 ns with 4 threads, so it wins the median but loses the 1-thread and 4-thread 99.9th percentile. Its own README (g++ 4.8.4, i7-2630QM, flags not given, microsecond timer) shows a 0.35 us average versus spdlog async 2.59 us at 1 thread.
status_note: Abandoned since 2017-03-08 (753 stars, 18 open issues); the MIT notice in both source files makes it copyable despite GitHub showing no license, and it is small enough to vendor and patch.
